title: Russian Revolution
description: 1917–1922 civil war in the Russian Empire
wiki_lead:
The Russian Revolution was a period of political and social change in Russia starting in 1917. This period saw Russia abolish its monarchy and adopt a socialist form of government following two successive revolutions and a civil war. It can be seen as the precursor to other revolutions that occurred in the aftermath of World War I, such as the German Revolution of 1918–1919. The Russian Revolution was a key event of the 20th century.
The Russian Revolution began with the February Revolution in 1917, in the midst of World War I. With the German Empire inflicting defeats on the Eastern Front and increasing logistical problems causing shortages of bread and grain, the Russian Army was losing morale, with large-scale mutiny looming. Officials were convinced that if Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, the unrest would subside. Nicholas stepped down on 15 March [O.S. 2 March], ushering in a provisional government led by the Duma (parliament). During the unrest, locals in Petrograd (now Saint Petersburg) formed Soviet councils. These councils did not initially oppose the new government, but they insisted on having influence over it and control of the militias. By March, Russia had two rival governments. The Provisional Government held state power in military and international affairs, whereas the network of Soviets held domestic power. The working and urban middle classes provided critical support to the Soviets. There were mutinies, protests and strikes. Socialist and other leftist political organizations competed for influence within the Provisional Government and Soviets. Factions included the Mensheviks, Socialist Revolutionaries, Anarchists, and the Bolsheviks, a far-left party led by Vladimir Lenin.
The Bolsheviks won popularity with a program promising peace, land, and bread: an end to the war, land for the peasantry, and ending famine. After assuming power, the Provisional Government continued fighting the war in spite of public opposition. Taking advantage, the Bolsheviks and other factions gained popular support to advance the revolution. Responding to discontent in Petrograd, the Provisional Government repressed protestors, leading to the July Days. The Bolsheviks merged workers' militias loyal to them into the Red Guards. The volatile situation reached its climax with the October Revolution, an armed Bolshevik insurrection in Petrograd beginning 7 November [O.S. 25 October] that overthrew the Provisional Government. The Bolsheviks established their own government and proclaimed the establishment of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR). Under pressure from German military offensives, the Bolsheviks relocated the capital to Moscow. The RSFSR began reorganizing the empire into the world's first socialist state, practicing soviet democracy on a national and international scale. Their promise to end Russia's participation in World War I was fulfilled when Bolshevik leaders signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in March 1918. The Bolsheviks also established the Cheka, a secret police and revolutionary security service working to uncover, punish, and eliminate those considered to be "enemies of the people" in a series of campaigns called the Red Terror.
Although the Bolsheviks held large support in urban areas, they had foreign and domestic enemies that refused to recognize their government. Russia erupted into a bloody civil war, which pitted the Reds (Bolsheviks) against an array of enemies, which included nationalist movements, anti-Bolshevik socialist parties, anarchists, monarchists and liberals; the latter two parties strongly supported the Russian White movement which was led mainly by right-leaning officers and seen as fighting for the restoration of the imperial order. The Bolshevik commissar Leon Trotsky began organizing workers' militias loyal to the Bolsheviks into the Red Army. While key events occurred in Moscow and Petrograd, every city in the empire was convulsed, including the provinces of national minorities, and in the rural areas peasants took over and redistributed land.
As the war progressed, the RSFSR established Soviet power in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Byelorussia, Georgia, and Ukraine. Wartime cohesion and intervention from foreign powers prompted the RSFSR to begin unifying these nations under one flag and created the Soviet Union. Historians consider the end of the revolutionary period to be in 1922, when the civil war concluded with the defeat of the White Army and separatist factions, leading to mass emigration from Russia. The victorious Bolshevik Party reconstituted itself into the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and remained in power for six decades.

grok_lead: The Russian Revolution of 1917 encompassed two principal upheavals: the February Revolution (March in the Gregorian calendar), which forced the abdication of Tsar Nicholas II on March 15, ending three centuries of Romanov rule and establishing a Provisional Government, and the October Revolution (November Gregorian), during which Bolshevik forces under Vladimir Lenin overthrew that government in Petrograd on October 25 (November 7 Gregorian). These events dismantled the Russian Empire's autocratic structure amid World War I's strains, including military defeats, food shortages, and industrial disruptions that fueled strikes and soldier mutinies. Rooted in long-standing grievances against absolutism, serfdom's legacy, and rapid industrialization's inequalities, the revolutions reflected deeper societal fractures exacerbated by the war's toll of over 2 million Russian deaths by early 1917. The Provisional Government's failure to end the war or enact land reforms alienated peasants and workers, enabling the Bolsheviks âadvocating "peace, land, and bread"âto gain support through soviets (workers' councils) and military committees. Historians like Richard Pipes characterize the October phase not as a broad popular uprising but as a targeted seizure of power by a disciplined vanguard, initiating civil war, the Red Terror, and a totalitarian regime that suppressed dissent and collectivized society at immense human cost. The revolutions' legacy includes the Soviet Union's formation in 1922, the spread of communist ideology globally, and profound geopolitical shifts, though they resulted in millions of deaths from famine, executions, and conflict, underscoring the causal link between Bolshevik authoritarianism and subsequent tyrannies. Despite romanticized narratives in some academic traditions, primary accounts and empirical analyses reveal the events' violent, ideologically driven nature, with the Bolshevik consolidation prioritizing state control over democratic aspirations.
